parsed.rationale: Both `DiscogsMarkupParser.ResolvedToken` (line 89, `DiscogsMarkupParser.swift`) and `ResolvedBioToken` (line 20, `ResolvedBioToken.swift`) are `type-alias-union` declarations in the same `Metadata` package with identical structure (`shared_field_count: 9`, `jaccard: null` indicating exact match). Neither record carries any test, codegen, mock, or sample-app flag, so the duplication is not intentional by policy. Maintaining two names for the same 9-case union type creates silent divergence risk: a future change to one alias will not automatically propagate to the other, and consumers may inadvertently depend on the nested name `DiscogsMarkupParser.ResolvedToken` rather than the public top-level `ResolvedBioToken`.

specifics.proposed_action: Determine which of the two type aliases is the canonical definition and delete the other, updating all call sites to use the surviving name. Given that `ResolvedBioToken` lives in its own dedicated file (`ResolvedBioToken.swift`) and has a top-level, non-nested name, it is the better candidate to keep. `DiscogsMarkupParser.ResolvedToken` (line 89 of `DiscogsMarkupParser.swift`) should be replaced with a `typealias ResolvedToken = ResolvedBioToken` inside `DiscogsMarkupParser` — or removed entirely — so that the single shared-field-count-9 union type is defined exactly once in the `Metadata` package.
specifics.why_no_category_fits: Both records are `type-alias-union` declarations in the same package (`Metadata`), not conforming types or protocols, so none of the structured categories (protocol-inheritance, default-implementation, generic-parameterization, subclass-lift, etc.) apply. The duplication is a straightforward alias-vs-alias redundancy: one nested alias inside `DiscogsMarkupParser` and one top-level alias in a dedicated file define the same 9-case union. The correct fix is a simple deduplication/redirect, which is closer to 'extract-to-common' in spirit but does not require moving anything to a new package — both already live in `Metadata`. 'extract-to-common' would misrepresent the action because no cross-package extraction is needed.
